title: Boolean Derivative Certificates and Maximal ANF Terms
pages:
Electronic Colloquium on Computational Complexity, Report No. 83 (2026)

      Boolean Derivative Certificates and Maximal ANF Terms
                                                  Nicholas Smirnov

                       Department of Computer Science, Stony Brook University


                                                         Abstract
      For a Boolean function f   : {0, 1}n → {0, 1}, the higher-order Boolean derivative D       S f computes the
      parity of f over each S-dimensional subcube. We prove that DS f ≡ 1 exactly when S is a maximal
      monomial support in the algebraic normal form of f . This correspondence motivates the derivative
      certificate depth ∆∂ ( f ), defined as the minimum degree of a nonempty maximal algebraic normal form
      monomial. We study the decision problem BCD: given f and k, decide whether ∆∂ ( f ) ≤ k. We show
      that this problem is coNP-complete for every fixed constant k ≥ 1, NP-complete when k = n, and
      belongs to Σ2⊕ P when k is part of the input; in the variable-k case it is also both NP-hard and coNP-hard.
      These results identify the ∃∀⊕ upper bound and leave Σ2⊕ P -completeness as an open problem.


1   Introduction
The algebraic normal form (ANF) of a Boolean function f , its unique representation as an F2 -multilinear
polynomial, has been quite foundational to Boolean function theory since Zhegalkin [17]. The supports of
the monomials in the ANF form a finite subset of 2[n] . Its inclusion-maximal elements form an antichain
and encode the top-level algebra of f .
    Boolean derivatives, systematized by Thayse [14], offer another perspective. The first-order derivative Di f
measures sensitivity of f to flipping xi , while DS f tests simultaneous sensitivity to all of S. Applications
include test generation [11], formal verification [16], and circuit complexity [6].
    The main equivalence connecting these two objects does not appear to be widely emphasized in the
literature:
                      DS f ≡ 1     ⇐⇒      S is a maximal ANF monomial support of f .
The condition DS f ≡ 1 is a parity certificate for satisfiability, it guarantees that every S-dimensional subcube
contains an odd number of satisfying assignments, hence at least one. We call S a constant derivative
certificate. Whenever such a nonempty certificate exists, it gives stronger evidence for satisfiability than a
single point witness: the subcube-parity condition holds universally over all 2n−|S| base vectors b, whereas
a point witness is a single evaluation. We define ∆∂ ( f ) as the minimum cardinality of a constant derivative
certificate.
    We study the decision problem BCD: does f admit a constant derivative certificate of size ≤ k? Its
natural ∃∀⊕ formulation separates the analysis into three cases: fixed k, where the problem is coNP-
complete; k = n, where it is NP-complete; and variable k, where it lies in Σ2⊕P .

Related work. Boolean derivatives appear in Boolean difference calculus, including Thayse’s mono-
graph [14], and in applications such as test generation [11], formal verification [16], and symmetric
cryptography [2]. Polynomial representations of Boolean functions over finite fields are foundational in
algebraic approaches to circuit lower bounds, including the Razborov–Smolensky method [10, 12]. Toda’s
theorem [15] shows the uses of counting and parity in complexity theory. The polynomial-time hierarchy
originates with Stockmeyer [13]; parity-oracle variants are related to work of Papadimitriou and Zachos [8].

Organization. Section 2 recalls Boolean derivatives and ANF. Section 3 proves the derivative–ANF
correspondence. Section 4 introduces derivative certificate depth. Sections 5–9 establish the complexity
results.

4   Constant Derivative Certificates
Definition 6. A nonempty set S ⊆ [n] is a constant derivative certificate for f if DS f ≡ 1. The derivative
certificate depth of f is
                           ∆∂ ( f ) := min |S| : ∅ ̸= S ⊆ [n], DS f ≡ 1 ,
                                           

with ∆∂ ( f ) = ∞ if no such S exists. By Theorem 4, ∆∂ ( f ) equals the minimum degree of a nonempty
maximal element of supp( f ).

Proposition 7. ∆∂ ( f ) < ∞ if and only if f is nonconstant.

Proof. If f ≡ 0: then supp( f ) = ∅, so no maximal element exists and ∆∂ ( f ) = ∞.
   If f ≡ 1: then c∅ = 1 and c T = 0 for all T ̸= ∅ (since Möbius inversion gives c∅ = f (0) = 1
and c{i} = f (0) ⊕ f (ei ) = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0, etc.). So supp( f ) = {∅}, whose unique element is empty. Since
Definition 6 requires a nonempty certificate, ∆∂ ( f ) = ∞.
   If f is nonconstant: supp( f ) contains at least one nonempty set. Since supp( f ) is a finite nonempty
poset, it has a maximal element S. If S = ∅, then every proper superset satisfies c T = 0, and c∅ = 1; but
then f ≡ 1 by Möbius inversion, contradicting nonconstancy. So S ̸= ∅, giving ∆∂ ( f ) ≤ |S| < ∞.

Remark 8. The proposition shows ∆∂ ( f ) = ∞ for both constant functions, even though f ≡ 1 is satisfiable.
The parameter ∆∂ does not measure satisfiability.

5    Examples
Example 9 (Linear functions). If f = xi1 ⊕ · · · ⊕ xik , the ANF consists of k degree-one monomials
{i1 }, . . . , {ik }, each of which is maximal, since no higher-degree monomial appears. Hence ∆∂ ( f ) = 1.
Example 10 (Pure conjunction). f = x1 · · · xk has a single ANF monomial [k], which is trivially maximal.
Hence ∆∂ ( f ) = k, showing that the parameter can equal the degree of the unique maximal ANF monomial.

Example 11 (Majority on three variables). f = x1 x2 ⊕ x1 x3 ⊕ x2 x3 . Möbius inversion gives c{1,2,3} =

Example 12 (Constant functions). ∆∂ ( f ) = ∞ for f ≡ 0 and f ≡ 1 by Proposition 7.

8    The Unrestricted Case: k = n
Theorem 15. BCD with k = n is NP-complete.
Proof. When k = n, the condition ∆∂ ( f ) ≤ n is equivalent, by Proposition 7, to f being nonconstant (since
every nonempty monomial has degree ≤ n).
    NP-membership. A pair of assignments a, b ∈ {0, 1}n with f ( a) ̸= f (b) is a polynomial-time verifiable
witness for nonconstancy.
    NP-hardness. We reduce S AT to nonconstancy. Given φ(y1 , . . . , ym ), introduce a variable z and define
f (y1 , . . . , ym , z) := z · φ(y1 , . . . , ym ).
    If φ is unsatisfiable, then φ ≡ 0 as a Boolean function, so f ≡ 0 is constant. If φ is satisfiable with
witness a ∈ {0, 1}m , then f ( a, 0) = 0 ̸= 1 = f ( a, 1), so f is nonconstant. The reduction runs in polynomial
time.

Remark 16. The transition from coNP to NP as k grows is quite interesting. In (∗), the ∀-layer ranges over
2n−k base vectors: at fixed k this is exponential, making the ∀-layer the bottleneck; at k = n it ranges over
{0, 1}0 = {()}, a single empty tuple, making it vacuous. As k increases, the ∀-layer collapses and the
complexity seems to go from coNP toward NP.

The Derivative Lattice
The family of all higher-order derivatives of f can be organized as the derivative lattice: nodes are the
derivatives DS f for S ⊆ [n], ordered by inclusion of S, with an edge from DS f to DS∪{i} f whenever i ∈   / S.
Level k contains exactly (nk) nodes, the derivatives of order k. This is actually the Hasse diagram of the
Boolean lattice 2[n] , shown by the fact that the operators Di commute: the node reached by applying Di
then D j is the same as the node reached by applying D j then Di .
   In this picture, Theorem 4 says that a node DS f is accepting (identically 1) if and only if S is a maximal
ANF monomial support of f . The derivative certificate depth ∆∂ ( f ) is then the minimum level containing
an accepting node. Figure 1 illustrates this for n = 3.
